Year / Time Period.text: 2003–2004, Seven consecutive months, on the 7th day of each month, 10 AM–10 PM.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Cafe Konj was a series of long-duration performances in the public space of a cafe in central Tehran.
Created to establish direct communication with an audience outside the realm of art.

For the artist, this project was a process of understanding and defining the concept of performance art and rethinking her own position as an artist; this was during a period when this medium was still unknown or unfamiliar to her and her audience, and access to theoretical and visual resources was very limited.
Throughout these performances, the artist tried to share the understanding she was gaining of this medium unmediated with the audience; a process she herself describes as "reinventing the wheel."
Questions such as "What does art want?", "What does the audience want?" and "Can non-traditional media connect with people?" took shape at the core of this experience.

sections.title: Context & Site
paragraphs: This series was performed in a small cafe in downtown Tehran (near Keshavarz Boulevard and Valiasr Square); a space that at the time was located outside the popular artistic neighborhoods, and its audience primarily consisted of passersby and returning regulars.
In 2003, Tehran’s city center lacked spaces such as galleries and cultural cafes, and such spaces were mostly concentrated in northern Tehran.
For the artist, executing the project in this location was a conscious choice, distancing from the official art spaces, and a move towards an urban and informal context.

sections.title: Motivations & Questions
paragraphs: This project took shape during a period when "conceptual art" was being consolidated with the support of official institutions, and new structures of control and direction in Iranian contemporary art were gradually forming.

For Jinoos Taghizadeh, "Cafe Konj Performances" was an effort to distance herself from this atmosphere and to move towards direct communication with the general public, a public that existed outside the official art system.

Simultaneously, the formation of this project was connected to prior experiences with independent movements in the 1990s and encountering the cultural policies of the reform period; a period that, according to the artist, despite its open and progressive facade, was producing a kind of controlled cultural showcase.
In this context, the project was conceived as an attempt to move past this "showcase vitrine" and to return to the city and everyday life.

sections.title: Constraints & Strategies
paragraphs: These performances were conducted without obtaining official permits and outside of institutional structures.

After a few performances, some signs of security surveillance emerged, but there was no clear mechanism/procedure to obtain a permit anyway, as such a medium was fundamentally undefined within the administrative structure.
Faced with this situation, the project continued without navigating official channels, leaving the responsibility for any potential stoppage to the supervisory bodies.
The lack of a financial sponsor, while a limitation, allowed for complete independence in decision-making.
Furthermore, the social conditions of that period, compared to more recent years, allowed for a freer space to execute the project.

sections.title: Fundings & Partners
paragraphs: With the collaboration and trust of the cafe owners (Sattar Afshar and Maryam Monjezi).
The project was self-funded.

sections.title: About the Artist
paragraphs: Jinoos Taghizadeh (born 1971, Tehran) is a multimedia artist.

She studied Dramatic Literature at the Niavaran Cultural Center and Sculpture at the University of Tehran, and began her artistic career in various fields, such as set design, screenwriting, puppet theater, and children's illustration.
She subsequently collaborated with various publications inside and outside of Iran as a critic, essayist, and art editor.

In her practice, she utilizes diverse media including drawing, painting, sculpture, installation, video/audio, performance, olfactory (relating to the sense of smell) installation, participatory art, and artist's books.
In her working method, there are no boundaries between disciplines, nor between research and presentation.

Over the past three decades, Taghizadeh has exhibited her works internationally at biennials, museums, and art centers, while simultaneously, as a civil activist, defining her art in close connection with her social and political concerns.
She has been residing in Toronto since 2022 and continues her studies in the field of creative writing.

Audience participation in this series of performances varied and depended on each specific performance.
In some instances, the audience was placed in the position of an active participant, while in others, they were merely observers or listeners.

In the first performance, the artist, wearing a birdcage on her head and while playing the sound of a canary singing, sold poetry oracles by Hafez (14 century Iranian Poet (1325–1390)), and the audience interacted with her just as they would when encountering an urban street vendor of Faals.
In another performance, the continuous reading of a handmade book in a space covered with yarn placed the audience in a position of listening and dealing with a disruption of their concentration.

In a performance that coincided with the anniversary of the beginning of the Iran-Iraq War, the act of bandaging expanded over bodies, objects, and even the exterior space of the cafe, while the audience was suddenly confronted with this very situation.
In the performance called "The Journey to Paradise", the audience participated in the construction of the piece by writing letters to the dead or entrusting objects.
In the Nowruz (Persian New Year) performance, which involved Goldfish, some audience members were indirectly invited to draw and further engaged in the action.
In the "Long Live Joseph Beuys" performance, an unexpected encounter occurred with audience members who viewed the artist in the role of a healer.

In the final performance, by offering "Qajar Coffee" (a historical reference to assassination by poisoned coffee), by collecting signatures from the audience, they participated in making a conscious decision to consume a "poisoned" drink, which made them sick.

Throughout these seven months, audiences generally engaged with the project with a high level of trust, and even when faced with disturbing or challenging situations, they did not display oppositional reactions.
